engine-and-fadec/0/p1.context: System note 'Engine and FADEC', section 'What it is', paragraph
engine-and-fadec/0/p1.text: AW169 Standard has the PW210A; AW169 EP has the PW210A1. The two engines are physically identical — the only difference is FADEC software, which raises the available power (AEO and OEI) and changes the limits. There is no hardware change between them.
engine-and-fadec/0/p1.note: RFM EP Section 7 p.7-565 (Chap 71, Power Plant): 'The engine PW210A1 differs from the PW210A only for increased performances (both AEO and OEI)... Differences... is only due to a different FADEC software... without any hardware change.' Confirmed verbatim.

engine-and-fadec/2/p0.context: System note 'Engine and FADEC', section 'The ENG MODE knob', paragraph
engine-and-fadec/2/p0.text: One rotary switch per engine on the Engine Control Panel, with detented fixed positions — OFF, IDLE, FLT — so it holds position without being watched. Getting to OFF takes two deliberate actions (push down, then rotate) to prevent an accidental shutdown. Engine 1's knob is labelled IDLE/APU, because engine 1 can be run in APU mode to provide power on the ground without the main rotor turning at flight speed.
engine-and-fadec/2/p0.note: RFM EP Section 7 p.7-580/581 (Chap 76, Engine Controls, Figure 7-216 key, ref 1/3): 'ENG 1(2) MODE rotary switch - OFF/IDLE/FLT fixed positions... Two distinct actions (push down and rotate) are required to select OFF position... for Engine #1 the IDLE/APU label is presented in place of IDLE only.' Confirmed verbatim (this description is not duplicated in the Standard RFM text dump, but the switch and panel are shared hardware per the engine-and-fadec/0/p1 no-hardware-change finding, and the AW169 EP RFM Section 7 Chap 76 is the authoritative system description source for this shared panel).

engine-and-fadec/6/p2.context: System note 'Engine and FADEC', section '1(2) ENG FAIL FIXED', paragraph
engine-and-fadec/6/p2.text: How the affected engine is shut down depends on where its torque froze: at or below 50%, it can be left running to touchdown (then lower collective smoothly to MPOG, watching NR — shut it down first if NR rises above limit); above 50%, and especially above Maximum Continuous Power, it has to be shut down — within 5 minutes if above MCP — before the approach, expecting NR droop and a large torque split as it spools down.

engine-and-fadec/4/p0.context: System note 'Engine and FADEC', section 'Starting', paragraph
engine-and-fadec/4/p0.text: The brushless starter-generator turns the engine for the start (see the Electrical Power System note). A CRANK switch per engine drives a dry motoring cycle. Duty-cycle limits: after the first start attempt wait 30 seconds, after the second another 30 seconds, after the third wait 30 minutes. Motoring is one of 45 s on / 10 min off, 30 s on / 5 min off, or 15 s on / 2 min off — repeatable three times, then a 30-minute rest.
engine-and-fadec/4/p0.note: RFM p.1-21 STARTER DUTY CYCLE: matches word for word (30s/30s/30min start attempts; 45s/10min, 30s/5min, 15s/2min motoring cycles, repeat 3x then 30min rest).

engine-and-fadec/7/p0.context: System note 'Engine and FADEC', section '1(2) ENG IDLE', paragraph
engine-and-fadec/7/p0.text: Audio tone and voice, ground only. It means power was demanded with an engine not ready to give it: a take-off begun with an engine still at IDLE, or an ENG MODE knob at IDLE with the collective not fully down, or engine 1 still in APU mode. Reduce collective to minimum pitch on ground, then bring the affected knob back to FLT. If engine 1 was in APU mode, set its knob to IDLE and its ACC switch to MAIN first, wait for the accessory-drive transition to complete on the MFD, then select FLT.
engine-and-fadec/7/p0.note: FIXED: 'DRIVE switch' -> 'ACC switch'. RFM p.3-19 (1(2) ENG IDLE procedure) names the switch 'ENG 1 ACC switch', confirmed at multiple other RFM pages (e.g. p.2-26 step 3, p.2-84 CAS state list). Audio tone + voice ground-only, MPOG, APU-mode sub-steps all otherwise match p.3-19 exactly.

engine-and-fadec/6/p1.text: The problem is a torque split: with one engine's power frozen and the other following the rotor, the two torques diverge. A split over 30% brings up the 1(2) ENG DEGR caution on the higher-torque engine. Below that, monitor and land as soon as practicable. During descent, do not let the good engine's torque fall below 10%.

electrical-system/0/p0.context: System note 'Electrical Power System (EPGDS)', section 'What it is', paragraph
electrical-system/0/p0.text: The Electrical Power Generation and Distribution System (EPGDS) generates AC power, converts it to 28 VDC, and distributes it. There is no usable AC bus — AC exists only internally between the generators and their control units; every load on the aircraft is 28 VDC.
electrical-system/0/p0.note: Matches the independently-verified AW169 EP System Note wording verbatim (shared EPGDS architecture).

electrical-system/0/p1.context: System note 'Electrical Power System (EPGDS)', section 'What it is', paragraph
electrical-system/0/p1.text: Generation is two brushless starter-generators, one per engine. During start they run as motors, turning the engine; once the engine is running they generate. Each is managed by its own Brushless Control Unit (BCU) in the rear fuselage under the cargo compartment — the BCU does the AC-to-28VDC conversion in generation mode and the reverse in start mode.

electrical-system/0/p2.context: System note 'Electrical Power System (EPGDS)', section 'What it is', paragraph
electrical-system/0/p2.text: Two Nickel-Cadmium batteries in the rear avionic bay: a 33 Ah main battery (MAIN BATT) and a 13 Ah auxiliary battery (AUX BATT). Optional kits substitute higher-capacity units (44 Ah main; 28 Ah or 33 Ah auxiliary). The batteries start the engines when no ground power is connected, and are the sole power source after a double generator failure. On the ground the system can instead be fed by a DC Ground Power Unit — recommended for engine starts after a cold soak.

electrical-system/0/p3.context: System note 'Electrical Power System (EPGDS)', section 'What it is', paragraph
electrical-system/0/p3.text: Distribution is solid-state (SSEPM): instead of a wall of mechanical circuit breakers and relays, power is routed through Remote Electrical Power Units (REPUs) — two in the nose compartment, one in the rear fuselage — fed from two DC Power Distribution Units (DC PDU 1 and DC PDU 2) in the rear avionic bay. The DC PDUs do the contactor switching, bus voltage and current monitoring, and over/under-voltage and overcurrent protection. A conventional Circuit Breaker Panel on the overhead console still feeds the emergency buses directly.

electrical-system/1/p0.context: System note 'Electrical Power System (EPGDS)', section 'Controls', paragraph
electrical-system/1/p0.text: The electrical control panel in the interseat console carries: GEN 1, GEN 2, MAIN BATT, BATT AUX, EXT PWR, and the MASTER CUT OFF SWITCH (MCOS). GEN switches have an ON, a RESET, and an OFF position — RESET is how a tripped generator is brought back on line.
electrical-system/1/p0.note: Matches the independently-verified AW169 EP System Note wording verbatim.

electrical-system/2/p0.context: System note 'Electrical Power System (EPGDS)', section 'The bus structure', paragraph
electrical-system/2/p0.text: GEN 1 normally feeds MAIN BUS 1 and MAIN BUS 3; GEN 2 feeds MAIN BUS 2 and MAIN BUS 4. Below the main buses sit six NON ESSENTIAL buses (comfort and mission loads — cabin lighting, sockets, wipers, EFB power, external camera, OPLS, and so on).
electrical-system/2/p0.note: Matches the independently-verified AW169 EP System Note wording verbatim.

electrical-system/2/p1.context: System note 'Electrical Power System (EPGDS)', section 'The bus structure', paragraph
electrical-system/2/p1.text: The Emergency Subsystem is the part that survives a total generation loss: EMERGENCY BUS 1 and 2 (fed from the Circuit Breaker Panel) and ESSENTIAL BUS 1 and 2 (REPU 1 and 2, Channel B). These carry the irreducible minimum — engine controls and ignition, FADEC channel B, both fire detection and extinguisher circuits, landing-gear control, fuel shut-off valves, standby ADI, one AFCS flight control computer per side, one ADAHRS, VHF 1, and the pilot's PFD/MFD. A number of items on these buses are marked as available on the ground only, i.e. lost in flight after a double generator failure.

electrical-system/4/p2.context: System note 'Electrical Power System (EPGDS)', section 'The OVRD switches on the EDCU ELEC page', paragraph
electrical-system/4/p2.text: GEN BUS — in a double generator failure, OVRD connects battery power to MAIN BUS 1 (again trading battery endurance for the loads on that bus).

electrical-system/4/p0.context: System note 'Electrical Power System (EPGDS)', section 'The OVRD switches on the EDCU ELEC page', paragraph
electrical-system/4/p0.text: BUS TIE — OVRD ties the two generators' distribution together so they share the total electrical load. It is the response to a DC GENERATOR OVERLOAD (1(2) DC GEN OVLD — set by more than 100% for over 45 seconds, or more than 75% for over 10 minutes). In a double generator failure it has a second use: with the generators gone, BUS TIE OVRD extends battery power to MAIN BUS 2, at the cost of shorter battery endurance.

electrical-system/4/p1.context: System note 'Electrical Power System (EPGDS)', section 'The OVRD switches on the EDCU ELEC page', paragraph
electrical-system/4/p1.text: NON ESS L and NON ESS R — after a single generator failure the non-essential buses drop. NON ESS L to OVRD restores NON ESS BUS 1 and 3; NON ESS R to OVRD restores NON ESS BUS 2 and 4 — used only if a load on one of them is actually needed, since it adds to the surviving generator.

electrical-system/5/p0.context: System note 'Electrical Power System (EPGDS)', section 'Losing one generator', paragraph
electrical-system/5/p0.text: 1(2) DC GEN FAIL — reset the affected generator (RESET, then confirm ON); if it stays failed, switch it off and let the other one carry the load. With BUS TIE CLOSED the remaining generator supplies power and only the non-essential buses are lost; if BUS TIE stays OPEN (try BUS TIE RESET on the EDCU ELEC page first), the affected generator's main buses (1 and 3, or 2 and 4) are lost as well as all non-essential buses. Non-essential buses can be brought back selectively with the NON ESS L/R OVRD switches. Watch the surviving generator's load on the MFD and reduce electrical load if the limit is exceeded.

electrical-system/6/p0.context: System note 'Electrical Power System (EPGDS)', section 'Losing both generators — ELEC FAIL', paragraph
electrical-system/6/p0.text: A double DC generator failure triggers the "WARNING WARNING" aural and the ELEC FAIL warning. fire-protection/0/p2.context: System note 'Fire Protection', section 'What it is', paragraph
fire-protection/0/p2.text: Engine extinguishing is two identical, interchangeable stainless-steel bottles charged with HALON 1301 and nitrogen, mounted between the engine ejectors under the rear fairing. They are cross-connected: either bottle can be fired into either engine bay. Each bottle has a temperature-compensated pressure sensor that drives a low-pressure caption.

electrical-system/6/p2.context: System note 'Electrical Power System (EPGDS)', section 'Losing both generators — ELEC FAIL', paragraph
electrical-system/6/p2.text: If a load on MAIN BUS 1 is genuinely required, GEN BUS to OVRD feeds it from the battery — and BUS TIE to OVRD additionally feeds MAIN BUS 2 — but each override shortens the 30 minutes. The landing gear control is on a bus that is lost in flight in this state, so the gear has to be put down with the LANDING GEAR EMERGENCY DOWN procedure; VHF 1 is selected on the right side to keep radio contact. A subsequent MAIN BATT OFF caution means land as soon as possible, without qualification.

fire-protection/1/p0.context: System note 'Fire Protection', section 'What an engine fire looks like', paragraph
fire-protection/1/p0.text: An ENG 1(2) FIRE gives, together: the CAS warning message, the "ENG 1(2) FIRE" audio tone with the master warning flashing, a red FIRE light on the fire control panel, a red warning light on that engine's control panel, and the engine silhouette turning red on the MFD PWR PLANT format.

electrical-system/7/p0.context: System note 'Electrical Power System (EPGDS)', section 'Related failures', paragraph
electrical-system/7/p0.text: 1(2) EMER BUS FAIL — a single emergency bus is lost while generation is otherwise normal. The losses are specific and worth knowing: EMER BUS 1 takes VHF 1, the standby instrument (ESIS), engine 1 fire detection and extinguisher, and AFCS force-trim release; EMER BUS 2 takes the pilot's EDCU, PFD, master warning/caution lights, landing light, RAD ALT 2, engine 2 fire detection and extinguisher, NAV 2, GPS 2, and the transponder. Reduce speed and continue attentive.

weather-radar/0/p0.context: System note 'Weather Radar RTA-4112', section 'What it is', paragraph
weather-radar/0/p0.text: A fully automatic radar that displays significant weather data at all available ranges and altitudes, at all times, with a clutter-free display. evs-camera/0/p0.text: Two possible installations: the MAX-VIZ EVS-1500, IR image only, or the EVS-2300, which adds a color image alongside the IR one. A Long Wave Infrared camera is mounted facing forward under the right-hand nose compartment, feeding the MFD as a visual aid in reduced visibility. Selected on and off from the EDCU KITS → CAMERA tab; a video test pattern shows for about 5 seconds after power-on, then an OK message, then an IR image after about 20 seconds total.

evs-camera/1/p0.context: System note 'EVS Camera', section 'Display and field of view', paragraph
evs-camera/1/p0.text: Shown full-size on the MFD VIDEO page, or as picture-in-picture on VIDEO or DMAP pages. Brightness/contrast adjust via the VIDEO page bezel buttons — on the EVS-2300, the IR and color channels have independent brightness/contrast controls. Field of view (Narrow/Wide) is selected from the PFD EVS menu or the DCP EVS button, and on the EVS-2300 that selection applies to both the IR and color image together. Zooming is available via PFD controls or the DCP.

evs-camera/0/p1.context: System note 'EVS Camera', section 'What it is', paragraph
evs-camera/0/p1.text: The camera automatically recalibrates its IR sensor (NUC) every 4 minutes — a 1-second screen blank with CAL displayed — which can be inhibited from the same EDCU page if needed. It's self-anti-iced with internal heaters whenever powered on, fed from Main Bus 1 (REPU 1 Channel A), a bus not shown on the DC ELEC synoptic page.

ehps/0/p0.context: System note 'EHPS: Electric Motor-Driven Hydraulic Power Supply', section 'What it is', paragraph
ehps/0/p0.text: A 28 VDC electric motor-driven hydraulic pump installed on hydraulic system 1, ground use only. It provides just enough hydraulic pressure to do the full-and-free flight-controls check on the servo-actuators before either engine — and its mechanically-driven hydraulic power supply — is even running. Controlled from the EDCU HYD page, powered from the helicopter battery, and limited by AMMC logic to 2 minutes of operation maximum. In flight, switching it on is inhibited by design.

htaws/0/p1.context: System note 'HTAWS: Terrain Awareness and Warning', section 'What it does', paragraph
htaws/0/p1.text: This configuration provides five operating modes: Mode 1 (excessive rate of descent), Mode 3 (descent after take-off or missed approach), Mode 4 (flight into terrain when not in landing configuration), Mode 5 (excessive downward deviation from an ILS glideslope), Mode 6 (altitude callout). There is no OFFSHORE option and no SAR mode on this configuration.
htaws/0/p1.note: FIXED: 'four operating modes' -> 'five operating modes', added missing Mode 6 (Altitude Callout). RFM Supplement 13 p.S13-2 (DOC PAGE 1664) lists exactly Mode 1, 3, 4, 5, 6 for this configuration, and confirms no OFFSHORE/SAR modes.

adi-stby-battery/0/p0.context: System note 'ADI STBY Emergency Battery', section 'What it is', paragraph
adi-stby-battery/0/p0.text: A dedicated Li-Ion battery, installed in the left side of the nose avionics bay, that automatically feeds the standby attitude indicator for at least 30 minutes after a total failure of the electrical generating system. It connects through the CB panel to EMER BUS 1, protected by a 7.5A ADI STBY circuit breaker — a self-contained backup for exactly one instrument, not the wider emergency bus.

adi-stby-battery/0/p1.context: System note 'ADI STBY Emergency Battery', section 'What it is', paragraph
adi-stby-battery/0/p1.text: Controlled by a Control Switch Annunciator on the right side of the interseat console, three positions: ARM (battery powered through EMER BUS 1, ready to supply output), OFF (disconnected from both EMER BUS 1 and the ADI STBY), and TEST (press and hold — checks state of charge is above 80% plus the internal heater and temperature monitoring; TEST illuminates green if it passes). The STBY annunciator itself lights amber whenever the battery is actually delivering power to the ADI.

external-hoist/0/p0.context: System note 'External Hoist Operations (Goodrich)', section 'What it is', paragraph
external-hoist/0/p0.text: A Goodrich hoist unit mounted on the right side of the cabin, in either a 290 ft or 165 ft usable-cable version, each with its own pendant. The pilot and copilot can operate the hoist from the collective grip; the Hoist Operator (HO) operates it from the control pendant, which also displays cable payout. Pilot control always overrides the HO's input. Maximum load: 249 kg (550 lb) above 0°C OAT, 227 kg (500 lb) at or below — maximum 2 persons plus equipment either way.

external-hoist/1/p0.context: System note 'External Hoist Operations (Goodrich)', section 'Key limitations', paragraph
external-hoist/1/p0.text: Minimum crew: one pilot plus one Hoist Operator. Load raising/lowering is permitted in a stationary hover or forward flight up to 45 KIAS (80 KIAS with the extended main footstep kit fitted). Maximum permissible bank angle with the cable extended is 20° — exceeding 15° of lateral pendulum angle relative to the helicopter's vertical axis can cause the overload clutch to slip, and that clutch is unlikely to function correctly if actually overloaded. Takeoff and landing with a suspended load on the hoist is prohibited.
external-hoist/1/p0.note: RFM Supplement 5 p.S5-16/17/18: 4800 kg max weight, 4600 kg/Supplement 30 threshold, 45/80 KIAS (footstep kit), 20 deg bank, 15 deg pendulum/clutch-slip warning, overload-clutch caution, T/O-landing prohibition all confirmed verbatim.

external-hoist/1/p1.context: System note 'External Hoist Operations (Goodrich)', section 'Key limitations', paragraph
external-hoist/1/p1.text: During hoist operations the pilot must either fly manually, or fly attentively if HOV and RHT (or ALT) modes are engaged — the autopilot is not a substitute for monitoring during a hoist operation. Maximum weight including the hoisted load is 4800 kg (above 4600 kg for takeoff/landing, the Supplement 30 increased-gross-weight configuration is required). The HO must be harnessed throughout, wear protective gloves, and guide the cable by hand.
external-hoist/1/p1.note: RFM Supplement 5 p.S5-13 (minimum crew: one pilot + one HO) and p.S5-18/S5-19 (autopilot fly-manually-or-attentive rule, HO harness/gloves/cable-guiding) confirmed verbatim.

external-hoist/2/p0.text: HOIST CBL FOUL: the cable isn't winding correctly onto the drum, motor stops automatically. Proceed in forward flight with the load suspended (same 45/80 KIAS limits), find a suitable site, hover and slowly descend to lay the load on the ground, then recover the cable manually.

external-hoist/3/p0.text: Where OEI hover performance capability is not required: the gross weight and hover height that would normally satisfy the Flyaway or Vertical Reject WAT charts may not actually give a safe flyaway or reject with a cable extended and a load hanging — that's a real, named caveat, not a generic warning. ehps/1/p0.context: System note 'EHPS: Electric Motor-Driven Hydraulic Power Supply', section 'Why it changes the start sequence', paragraph
ehps/1/p0.text: Without EHPS, engine 1 normally has to start in ACC (accessory) mode first, because the flight-controls check needs mechanically-driven hydraulic pressure that only comes from a running engine. EHPS removes that dependency: run the electric pump on the ground, do the flight-controls check off it, then engine 1 can be started directly in MAIN mode, either engine first. The equivalent flight-controls check step later in the normal Engines Start procedure is skipped, since it's already been done.
ehps/1/p0.note: RFM Supplement 42 p.S42-1/S42-3/S42-4: EHPS purpose, 2-minute AMMC-enforced limit, MAIN-mode start and skipped flight-controls-check step all confirmed verbatim.

external-hoist/4/p0.context: System note 'External Hoist Operations (Goodrich)', section 'If a double DC generator failure happens with a load on the hook', paragraph
external-hoist/4/p0.text: The hoist reverts to being powered by the main battery. If the battery is used to recover the load, the normal 30-minute battery endurance figure is not guaranteed once the hoist has drawn on it.

ehps/2/p0.context: System note 'EHPS: Electric Motor-Driven Hydraulic Power Supply', section 'The check itself', paragraph
ehps/2/p0.text: ELEC PUMP switch on, confirm HYD 1 pressure reads 80–120 bar (this is genuinely in the pump's normal red zone on the gauge — don't read that as a fault). Exercise the controls progressively and slowly: collective to about 50% then cyclic to full displacement, cyclic centered then collective to full displacement, then pedals to full displacement. Deselect ELEC PUMP when done — it also disengages on its own after 2 minutes regardless.
ehps/2/p0.note: RFM Supplement 42 p.S42-3: 80-120 bar red-zone note, control-exercise sequence (collective ~50% then cyclic full, cyclic centred then collective full, then pedals full), 2-minute auto-disengage all confirmed verbatim.

external-hoist/3/p1.context: System note 'External Hoist Operations (Goodrich)', section 'Engine failure in the hover with a load on the hook', paragraph
external-hoist/3/p1.text: Where OEI hover performance capability is required — meaning the aircraft is being flown at the weights defined on the hover-OGE 2.5-minute-OEI charts specifically to guarantee no rotor droop or height loss on an engine failure — maintain the collective pitch setting (2.5-minute OEI rating covers the hover) and raise the load into the cabin; raising a full-length load from fully extended takes about 2 minutes.
external-hoist/3/p1.note: RFM Supplement 5 p.S5-32/33 (Procedures when OEI hover performance capability is required): 'Maintain collective pitch setting', 2.5 min OEI rating, ~2 minutes to raise a full-length load from fully extended, all confirmed verbatim.

cargo-hook/4/p0.context: System note 'Cargo Hook Operations', section 'Engine failure in the hover with a load on the hook', paragraph
cargo-hook/4/p0.text: Same caveat as with the hoist: gross weights and hover heights that satisfy the standard Flyaway or Vertical Reject WAT charts may not actually give a safe flyaway or reject with an external load hanging underneath — it's a genuinely different situation from a clean aircraft, not just a heavier one. Recover aircraft control per the standard Vertical Reject or Flyaway procedure, then jettison the load and transition forward (maximum 45 KIAS) depending on conditions.

ditching/0/p0.context: System note 'Ditching Configurations', section 'What the system is', paragraph
ditching/0/p0.text: Two forward and two aft float installations in dedicated fuselage openings, two gas distribution/inflation systems, and four immersion switches. Demonstrated and approved for ditching up to Sea State 6 (significant wave height 4–6 m) at weights up to 4800 kg — well beyond the Sea State 4 that ditching regulations actually require.

cargo-hook/0/p0.context: System note 'Cargo Hook Operations', section 'What it is', paragraph
cargo-hook/0/p0.text: A cargo-only (Non-Human External Cargo) hook system, approved for Class B rotorcraft-load combinations — the load must be jettisonable and lifted free of land or water — Day VFR only, one pilot minimum, and only personnel actually involved in the cargo operation may be aboard. Powered from Main Bus 3; the emergency release circuit is on its own separate EMERG Bus 1, so it stays live even if the normal cargo hook power is lost.
cargo-hook/0/p0.note: RFM Supplement 6 p.S6-1 (NHEC/Class B definition, MAIN BUS 3 / EMERG BUS 1 power split) and p.S6-6 (Day VFR, one pilot, only personnel directly involved) confirmed verbatim.

cargo-hook/1/p0.context: System note 'Cargo Hook Operations', section 'Key limitations', paragraph
cargo-hook/1/p0.text: Maximum weight with the external load: 4800 kg. Airspeed: 100 KIAS up to 12,000 ft density/pressure altitude (whichever is lower), 90 KIAS above that — but airspeed is really governed by controllability, since load size, shape, and strop length all affect handling, and airspeed must always be adjusted to keep the load in continuous sight.
cargo-hook/1/p0.note: RFM Supplement 6 p.S6-7 (4800 kg) and p.S6-12 (100 KIAS up to 12000 ft HD/HP, 90 KIAS above, controllability caveat) confirmed verbatim.

ditching/0/p2.context: System note 'Ditching Configurations', section 'What the system is', paragraph
ditching/0/p2.text: Two liferafts are carried, in one of two configurations: Carry-On (a free-standing installation on the seat rails, deployed manually through a Type IV emergency exit; requires the 8-seat forward cabin kit and reduces passenger capacity from 8 to 7) or Sponson (a liferaft mounted on each sponson, activated from the cockpit via a handle above the pilots' heads or from a secondary handle on the leading edge of the sponson).
ditching/0/p2.note: FIXED: 'Carry-On (stowed on a seat...)' -> precise RFM wording (free-standing installation on seat rails); Sponson activation rewritten to include the primary cockpit handle the old text omitted (previously only mentioned the secondary external handle, and used the unsupported phrase 'water-side deployment'). Matches Section 7 p.7-659 and Supplement 11 p.S11A-5, and the already-fixed AW169 EP equivalent (with 'two configurations' correctly kept - unlike EP, the Standard RFM p.7-659 explicitly says 'two alternate liferaft installations', no integrated 12-pax EFS liferaft option).

ditching/2/p1.context: System note 'Ditching Configurations', section 'The ditching sequence', paragraph
ditching/2/p1.text: Approach: set the radar altimeter (height-over-water is notoriously hard to judge by eye, hence the specific caution to use RadAlt cues), wipers fast, pitot heat off, confirm FLOATS EMER armed, assess sea state and wind, establish a ditching heading and a descent profile that targets no more than 30 kt groundspeed at water contact, emergency lights on, alert everyone for impact, transmit final position, brace order over the PA, and — if power allows — establish a hover at a safe height first. Touch down cushioning the impact with the collective, aircraft level or slightly nose-up (5°), avoiding any rearward movement.

ditching/2/p0.context: System note 'Ditching Configurations', section 'The ditching sequence', paragraph
ditching/2/p0.text: Preliminary: brief crew and passengers, notify ATC, transponder to 7700, seatbelt sign on, secure loose equipment, cabin doors confirmed closed (they stay closed throughout — opening them lets in the water that would otherwise be kept out), mute HTAWS, inhibit the low-height aural, life vests and harnesses on and tightened.
ditching/2/p0.note: RFM Supplement 11 p.S11A-17 (DITCHING PROCEDURE, Preliminary steps 1-9): matches verbatim including the doors-stay-closed rationale.

adelt/0/p0.context: System note 'ADELT: Crash Position Indicator with Deployable ELT', section 'What it is', paragraph
adelt/0/p0.text: A locator beacon on the left side of the tail cone, containing its own transmitter and antenna, that ejects from the aircraft in a crash — automatically, or manually at the pilot's discretion. Once deployed it transmits on two channels for two different purposes. The standard swept tone on 121.5/243.0 MHz — the classic analog distress tone — runs until battery power is exhausted, typically around 48 hours. Separately, 406.025 MHz carries an encoded digital message of the aircraft's position, sourced from the GPS/FMS via ARINC, and runs for about 24 hours.

ditching/1/p0.context: System note 'Ditching Configurations', section 'Hard rules', paragraph
ditching/1/p0.text: The floatation system and liferafts exist for ditching only — floatation bags and liferafts must never be inflated in flight. Takeoff after ditching is prohibited. Total occupants, crew included, must not exceed 11 when forecast sea conditions along the route exceed 2.5 m significant wave height. With retractable bear paws fitted, the gear must be retracted before extended overwater flight. Bear paws, snow pads, and snow skis (Supplements 8, 45, 50) are explicitly listed as not compliant with ditching requirements — fit any of those and the ditching approval no longer applies.
ditching/1/p0.note: VERIFIED, no change needed (initially suspected an error, RFM confirms the claim as written): RFM Supplement 49 p.S49-3 confirms 'With retractable bear paws kit installed, landing gear must be retracted before undertaking extended flight overwater' - a DIFFERENT kit (Supplement 49) from the fixed Supplement 8 bear paws, which is what the disqualifying list (Supplements 8/45/50) refers to. Also confirmed: 2.5 m sea state / 11 occupants rule, takeoff-after-ditching prohibition, floats/liferafts-never-inflated-in-flight, and the S8/S45/S50 ditching-incompatibility statements.

adelt/2/p0.context: System note 'ADELT: Crash Position Indicator with Deployable ELT', section 'Self-test discipline', paragraph
adelt/2/p0.text: The self-test should not be run more often than monthly — running it more frequently shortens the battery's life. Notify the nearest ATC facility before testing, since the 121.5 MHz tone the test actually transmits will be treated as a valid distress signal by anyone monitoring it, test or not.
adelt/2/p0.note: RFM Supplement 15 p.S15-3: monthly self-test limit (battery life), notify-ATC-first note (121.5 MHz treated as valid distress signal) confirmed verbatim.

eaps/3/p0.context: System note 'EAPS: Engine Air Particle Separator', section 'Malfunction', paragraph
eaps/3/p0.text: 1(2) EAPS PRESS means the bleed-air shut-off valve for that engine is stuck — closed when it should be open, or open when it should be closed. Continue flight either way, but know what it costs you: with EAPS switched ON and the valve actually closed, separation is degraded because the ejector isn't getting bleed air. With EAPS switched OFF and the valve actually open, aircraft performance may not match the EAPS-OFF performance charts — use the EAPS-ON charts instead in that case.

fuel-transfer-pump/0/p0.context: System note 'Fuel Transfer Pump', section 'What it's for', paragraph
fuel-transfer-pump/0/p0.text: A single reversible pump, submerged in the LH tank sump, that can move fuel in either direction between the left and right main tanks through a pipeline routed via the existing intercommunication channel — no new tank wall interfaces. It self-primes in either direction within 10 seconds of power, self-stops once it can't pump any more fuel to the other side, and reports its health to the AMMC.
fuel-transfer-pump/0/p0.note: Matches the independently-verified AW169 EP System Note wording verbatim (shared fuel transfer pump kit).

fuel-transfer-pump/1/p1.context: System note 'Fuel Transfer Pump', section 'The one-way rule in OEI', paragraph
fuel-transfer-pump/1/p1.text: Direction and progress show as a green arrow over the FUEL XFER icon on EDCU, PFD and the MFD synoptic page, plus an advisory naming the direction ("FUEL XFER 1→2" or "2→1"). FUEL XFER COMPLETE displays for about 10 seconds once an OEI transfer finishes and the pump stops itself.
fuel-transfer-pump/1/p1.note: Matches the independently-verified AW169 EP System Note wording verbatim.

fuel-transfer-pump/2/p0.context: System note 'Fuel Transfer Pump', section 'Why unusable fuel becomes 0 kg', paragraph
fuel-transfer-pump/2/p0.text: Without this kit, fuel below the intercommunication channel in the tank tied to a failed engine simply can't reach the system and counts as unusable. With the Fuel Transfer Pump installed and used, that figure becomes 0 kg indicated for OEI — the pump is precisely what closes that gap. Below 160 kg is where this actually starts mattering; above that level the two tanks are already interconnected and balanced on their own.
fuel-transfer-pump/2/p0.note: Matches the independently-verified AW169 EP System Note wording verbatim.

fuel-transfer-pump/3/p0.context: System note 'Fuel Transfer Pump', section 'AEO limits and stopping conditions', paragraph
fuel-transfer-pump/3/p0.text: In AEO, transfer automatically stops the moment 1(2) FUEL LOW activates on the tank being drawn from — FUEL XFER STOPPED displays for about 10 seconds. In the two genuinely abnormal cases — a leak, or one engine burning fuel unevenly — don't use FUEL XFER unless FUEL LOW is already active on the low tank and the other tank's spare fuel is actually needed to finish the flight safely. The routine case is different: after unbalanced flight has returned to balanced, XFER can simply restore the tanks to even without any of that caution attached. On the ground, it can also be used to correct an unbalance created by single-point refueling below the intercommunication channel.
fuel-transfer-pump/3/p0.note: Matches the independently-verified AW169 EP System Note wording verbatim.

rnp-apch-lpv/0/p0.context: System note 'RNP APCH with LPV/LP Minima', section 'What it is', paragraph
rnp-apch-lpv/0/p0.text: Requires its own AMMS option file enabled. RNP approaches flown to LPV or LP minima (charted as RNAV(GPS) or RNAV(GNSS)) use Satellite Based Augmentation (SBAS) to fly an approach with vertical guidance down to a 200 ft decision height, with no airport-specific ground equipment required. LPV gives lateral and vertical angular guidance; LP gives lateral angular guidance paired with Baro-VNAV for the vertical path instead. The GNSS sensors feed the FMS pseudo-localizer (NLOC) and pseudo-glideslope (NGS) deviations that the AFCS actually couples to.
rnp-apch-lpv/0/p0.note: Matches the independently-verified AW169 EP System Note wording verbatim (shared Supplement 43).

rnp-apch-lpv/0/p1.context: System note 'RNP APCH with LPV/LP Minima', section 'What it is', paragraph
rnp-apch-lpv/0/p1.text: Approved for day/night VFR and IFR. Maximum glide path angle 9°. Minimum airspeed to engage APP mode for these minima is 45 KIAS, and AFCS IAS mode must be engaged below 50 KIAS. Maximum ROD approaching the missed approach point is 900 fpm. Maximum airspeed at DH is 130 KIAS below 5000 ft, reducing 2 kt per 1000 ft above that — and if PWR LIM illuminates on the way down, airspeed must be reduced enough to clear it before reaching DH.
rnp-apch-lpv/0/p1.note: Matches the independently-verified AW169 EP System Note wording verbatim.

rnp-apch-lpv/2/p0.context: System note 'RNP APCH with LPV/LP Minima', section 'Flying it', paragraph
rnp-apch-lpv/2/p0.text: Before the FAF: confirm the white LPV or LP advisory, DA(H) set per the approach chart, PERFINIT executed, VNAV phase at CRUISE before the vertical path capture, and TOD correctly computed and shown. Arm NAPP (and NDCL if a deceleration profile is used) on the AFCS panel. If above the FAF altitude, the FMS captures the vertical path in Baro-VNAV down to FAF altitude, then transitions to pseudo-LOC/pseudo-GS guidance inside 2 NM of the FAF.
rnp-apch-lpv/2/p0.note: Matches the independently-verified AW169 EP System Note wording verbatim.

rnp-apch-lpv/3/p0.context: System note 'RNP APCH with LPV/LP Minima', section 'What a GNSS problem actually costs you', paragraph
rnp-apch-lpv/3/p0.text: A single GNSS RAIM integrity failure, or one SBAS precision-approach channel going to standby, is annunciated in the RFM as a loss of GNSS redundancy, and the instruction is to continue the approach (the GNSS sensor checks SBAS integrity every 4 seconds and may recover automatically).
rnp-apch-lpv/3/p0.note: FIXED: 'redundancy is reduced, not lost' -> matches the RFM's own literal phrase 'Loss of GNSS redundancy - Continue Approach', confirmed at RFM Supplement 43 p.S43-8 (GNSS RAIM ABOVE LIMIT) and p.S43-9 (SBAS PA FAIL), matching the already-fixed AW169 EP wording.

rnp-apch-lpv/3/p1.context: System note 'RNP APCH with LPV/LP Minima', section 'What a GNSS problem actually costs you', paragraph
rnp-apch-lpv/3/p1.text: If SBAS precision mode is lost on both GNSS sensors at once, the outcome depends on whether Baro-VNAV minima are available for that approach. If they are, FMS deviations revert automatically to LNAV/VNAV and Baro-VNAV — LPV is replaced by VGP on the PFD — and the approach can continue in coupled mode by pressing APP or DCL again, unless the aircraft is already below 1000 ft AGL, in which case discontinue regardless. If Baro-VNAV minima are not available at all, there's no fallback — discontinue the approach outright.
rnp-apch-lpv/3/p1.note: Matches the independently-verified AW169 EP System Note wording verbatim (RFM Supplement 43 p.S43-10, dual-SBAS-loss procedure).
